content: 1. My employer and I have received non-monetary support for travel and conference attendance from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Society for Pediatric Infectious Diseases. I am affiliated with the Dube Queen College of Medicine in Blantyre, Malawi. I have no conflicts of interest to declare. 2. I have been involved in the development of the updated guidelines for Pediatric Emergency Triage, Assessment, and Treatment (ETAT). My work in this area continues. 3. Dr. Trevor Duke, from the University of Melbourne, Australia, has declared no conflicts of interest. 4. Dr. Mike English, affiliated with the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme in Nairobi, Kenya, has received research support from the Wellcome Trust to study the uptake of guidelines and training in Kenya, including components of ETAT. He has also been a grant holder for sub-contracted funds from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, originating from a DFID grant, to support guideline development in Kenya, including fluid resuscitation. He remains actively involved in the development of the ETAT+ training program, which is used in Kenya and other countries. All materials for this program are freely accessible, and he does not receive personal income or emoluments for this work. 5. Dr. Hans Hartmann, from Hanover Medical School in Germany, received an award of $500 from Nutricia Metabolics to serve as a technical expert on the ketogenic diet for epilepsy and to speak at the International PDE Consortium meeting in Barcelona in 2013. This meeting was supported by Nutricia, but he did not receive travel support. He also received an award of $400 from Nutricia to serve as a technical expert on lysine-restricted diets for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy and chaired a workshop at the 2014 European Metabolic Group meeting in Zurich. Nutricia supported this meeting and covered his travel expenses, but he did not receive any additional bursaries. 6. Dr. Tabish Hazir, from the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad, Pakistan, has declared no conflicts of interest. 7. Dr. Angelina Kakooza-Mwesige, from Makerere University College of Health Sciences in Kampala, Uganda, has received research support from the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health in the United Kingdom. This support, amounting to $1,000 in 2012 for a three-year project, was provided to the Research Unit, Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, to conduct training for undergraduate medical, nursing, and clinical students, as well as postgraduate pediatric trainees. She has not participated in any ETAT training or received financial or non-monetary support from this collaboration. 8. Dr. Niranjan “Tex” Kissoon, from the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada, has declared no conflicts of interest. 9. Dr. Mehretie Kokeb, from the University of Gondar in Ethiopia, has declared no conflicts of interest. 10. Dr. Christian Korff, from Geneva University Hospitals in Switzerland, received research support from UCB Pharma, Switzerland, amounting to CHF 2,000, which was paid to his research unit in 2014. 11. Dr. Eddie Lang, from the University of Calgary in Canada, served as a GRADE consultant to the National Transportation Safety Agency and Emergency Medical Services for Children (a U.S. federal agency) for the development of a guideline on prehospital management of seizures. He received $7,000 for the entire contract in 2011. He also served as a GRADE consultant to the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation, supporting all task forces, including post-arrest targeting of PaO2. This work is ongoing and considered significant funding. 12. Dr. Kyaw Linn, from Yangon Children’s Hospital in Myanmar, has declared no conflicts of interest. 13. Dr. Juan Manuel Lozano León, from Florida International University in Miami, USA, has declared no conflicts of interest. 14. Dr. Leyla Namzova-Baranova, from the Russian Academy of Medical Science in Moscow, Russian Federation, has declared no conflicts of interest. 15. Dr. Archana Patel, from Indira Gandhi Government Medical College in Nagpur, India, has declared no conflicts of interest. 16. Dr. Ida Safitri Laksono, from Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, has declared no conflicts of interest. 17. Dr. Sunit Singhi, from the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research in Chandigarh, India, has declared no conflicts of interest. 18. Dr. Manal Hassan Taha, from the Federal Ministry of Health in Khartoum, Sudan, has declared no conflicts of interest. 19. Dr. Ian Maconochie, from St. Mary’s Hospital in London, United Kingdom, has declared no conflicts of interest. 20. Dr. Peter Meaney, from the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, USA, has received grant funding from the American Heart Association and Ronald McDonald House Charities. His employer, the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), received $328,000 and $200,000, respectively, to support pediatric emergency training programs in Molepolole, Botswana, where he serves as medical director. 21. Dr. Charles Newton, from the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme in Nairobi, Kenya, has declared no conflicts of interest. 22. Dr. Rakesh Lodha, from the All-India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi, India, has declared no conflicts of interest. 23. Dr. Stephen Playfor, from the Royal Manchester Children’s Hospital in the United Kingdom, received honoraria for speaking at six Forte educational events organized by Baxter Healthcare PLC. He received £1,300 for each event. His unit began using Plasma-Lyte 148, a balanced intravenous electrolyte solution with dextrose, which attracted the company’s interest. He spoke at these events using his own independent material.
